mechanism_narrative: The sustained upward trend in RETAIL_REC mobility over the past four weeks, moving from -25.9% to -17.3%, indicates a continued recovery in consumer activity and willingness to engage in out-of-home leisure, leading to further increases in retail and recreation visits.
failure_condition: RETAIL_REC over the next 28 days is lower than over the last 28 days, indicating a reversal of the observed recovery trend.

mechanism_narrative: A significant rebound in WORKPLACES mobility, specifically the increase from -27.3% to -8.6% over the last two weeks, suggests a return to office-based work which will directly increase incidental retail and recreation visits during weekdays.
candidate_trigger: WORKPLACES rises by more than 5 points week-on-week for two consecutive weeks
failure_condition: Despite WORKPLACES rising by more than 5 points week-on-week for two consecutive weeks, RETAIL_REC over the next 14 days does not increase relative to the prior 14 days.

mechanism_narrative: The concurrent decrease in RESIDENTIAL mobility (from 14.9% to 10.1%) and increase in TRANSIT mobility (from -33.1% to -23.7%) indicates a clear shift away from staying at home and towards out-of-home activities requiring public transport, which will boost retail and recreation.
failure_condition: RETAIL_REC over the next 28 days is lower than over the last 28 days, despite RESIDENTIAL mobility continuing to fall and TRANSIT mobility continuing to rise.

mechanism_narrative: The recent decline in PARKS mobility (from -3.6% to -16.9% over two weeks), following an earlier peak, suggests a shift in outdoor activity patterns, potentially due to changing weather or seasonal factors, which could redirect leisure spending towards indoor retail and recreation.
candidate_trigger: PARKS mobility falls for two consecutive weeks after a period of increase
failure_condition: RETAIL_REC over the next 28 days decreases, despite the observed decline in PARKS mobility, indicating no substitution effect.

mechanism_narrative: The broad-based recovery across RETAIL_REC, TRANSIT, and WORKPLACES, coupled with declining RESIDENTIAL time, indicates an underlying easing of restrictions or increased public confidence, driving sustained growth in out-of-home activities and thus retail and recreation.
failure_condition: The average of RETAIL_REC, TRANSIT, and WORKPLACES over the next 28 days does not increase, or RESIDENTIAL mobility does not continue to decrease.

mechanism_narrative: The stabilization of GROCERY_PHARM mobility near baseline (-0.6% for the last two weeks) suggests that essential shopping patterns have normalized, freeing up discretionary time and spending for non-essential retail and recreation activities.
candidate_trigger: GROCERY_PHARM mobility remains within +/- 1 point of baseline for two consecutive weeks
failure_condition: RETAIL_REC over the next 14 days decreases, despite GROCERY_PHARM mobility remaining stable near baseline, indicating no shift in discretionary activity.

mechanism_narrative: As WORKPLACES mobility continues its strong recovery (from -27.3% to -8.6%), the concurrent decline in PARKS visits (from -3.6% to -16.9%) suggests a shift from outdoor leisure to structured work and associated urban activities, which often include retail and recreation.
candidate_trigger: WORKPLACES rises for two consecutive weeks while PARKS falls for two consecutive weeks
failure_condition: RETAIL_REC over the next 7 days decreases, despite WORKPLACES rising and PARKS falling for two consecutive weeks, indicating no substitution effect.

mechanism_narrative: The consistent increase in TRANSIT station mobility over the past four weeks (from -34.3% to -23.7%) indicates a growing comfort with public transportation and increased movement across the metropolitan area, directly facilitating more retail and recreation visits.
failure_condition: TRANSIT mobility over the next 28 days does not continue its upward trend, or RETAIL_REC does not increase despite rising TRANSIT mobility.
